core: what social media marketing is: using social media platforms to deliver content that drives engagement with a brand (OpenStax working definition, paraphrased with attribution); Investopedia's parallel: using social platforms to reach audiences, build relationships, and promote products or services

the platform idea: different platforms attract different audiences and favor different formats; choosing a platform is a targeting decision — stated factually, with no platform-specific recommendations
organic versus paid: brand profiles posted for free versus sponsored content the brand pays for (OpenStax); earned exposure versus paid advertising (Investopedia); original examples only
the content idea: posts, stories (disappear after about 24 hours), videos, and live streams — each named with one line
engagement: likes, comments, shares, and direct messages — what each is, and why brands monitor them as signals
consistency: regular presence builds an audience; keeping a social presence requires posting fresh content frequently, monitoring engagement, and responding (OpenStax)
the honest framing: social media is a megaphone with a feedback loop — one-way broadcasting versus multidirectional communication, and the brand's lack of complete control over the message (OpenStax)
supporting: social media marketing is one of the main forms of digital marketing, alongside search engine marketing, content marketing, email marketing, pay-per-click advertising, and SEO (CFI)
social media marketing can be cost-effective and highly targeted, but requires ongoing content and reputation management (Investopedia)
brands measure social media campaigns with engagement, reach, and conversion metrics (Investopedia); OpenStax names clicks, likes, and shares as measurable engagement metrics

claims.claim: Social media marketing is defined as using social media platforms to deliver content that drives engagement with a brand (OpenStax's Principles of Marketing working definition); Investopedia defines it in parallel as using social media platforms to reach audiences, build relationships, and promote products or services.

The major social platforms differ in who uses them and what they are built for — broad global audiences, younger segments, business professionals, and formats centered on short text, images, or video — so the platform a brand chooses is itself a decision about which audience to reach.

A brand's social presence has two tracks: organic content posted free to its own profile, and sponsored content the brand pays the platform to show to a wider audience, including people who do not follow it (OpenStax: marketers create brand profiles and also sponsored content that they pay for).

Social content comes in standard forms: posts that stay in the feed, stories (photos and videos that disappear after 24 hours), videos, and live streams that broadcast in real time and let companies engage directly with their community.

Engagement is what users do with a brand's content — click, like, comment, share, favorite — and marketers monitor it, join the conversations users start, and evaluate metrics such as clicks, likes, and shares to tune their campaigns; Investopedia adds reach and conversions as campaign metrics.

Social media allows direct, private communication between users and brands (direct messages), as part of the multidirectional communication that distinguishes social platforms from one-way advertising.

Keeping a social presence requires ongoing effort: dedicated people who post fresh content frequently, monitor engagement, and respond to comments; continuous creation of new and engaging content is the engine of the practice.

The honest framing: mass promotion such as advertising is one-way communication, while social platforms allow multidirectional communication between company, users, and brand communities — and brands do not have complete control over the message, since users can freely write comments that may harm a brand's reputation.

Social media marketing is one of the main forms of digital marketing, listed by CFI alongside search engine marketing, content marketing, email marketing, pay-per-click advertising, and search engine optimization.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Industry publications publish widely varying, vendor-produced statistics about social media engagement, follower counts, and ROI that conflict across surveys and years and are not independently audited.
positions: Marketing-industry sources publish quantitative claims about social media results that vary widely by survey and year.
Those figures are produced by vendors and associations and are not independently verifiable from primary data.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson makes no quantitative claims about social media results. Engagement mechanics and the organic/paid distinction are stated qualitatively, exactly as OpenStax and Investopedia describe them. Platform statistics in the sources are time-anchored (2021-2022 textbook data) and are not repeated in the lesson; the platform idea is stated as a general factual principle.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Sources differ on whether social media marketing is primarily about promotion or about relationship-building.
positions: OpenStax emphasizes delivering content that drives engagement with the brand.
Investopedia emphasizes reaching audiences, building relationships, and promoting products or services.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both formulations as parallel descriptions of the same practice, and builds the honest framing on the shared point that social communication is multidirectional.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The phase-2 machine-generated draft contained unverifiable statistics and generic 'social media is powerful' phrasing; those were cut rather than retained.
rightsIssues: All three sources are used REFERENCE_ONLY: facts synthesized and prose written fresh, no source wording reproduced. The OpenStax working definition and Investopedia parallel definition are paraphrased with attribution.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A open textbook (per subject source-map). openstax.org blocks direct fetching; read via Wayback Machine capture dated 2026-05-10 of the canonical section URL. Supports: the working definition ('using social media platforms to deliver content that drives engagement with your brand'); brand profiles versus sponsored content the brand pays for; platform differences in audience and format; posts, stories (photos/videos that disappear after 24 hours), video distribution, and live streaming; engagement mechanics (click, like, comment, favorite, share; metrics such as clicks, likes, shares); the requirement of posting fresh content frequently, monitoring engagement, and responding to comments; one-way advertising versus multidirectional social communication; and the lack of complete control over the message.
